title: Stained Glass
objective: After this level you can explain how stained glass windows were made and what they taught.
summary: Glass was colored with metal oxides, cut, painted, fired and joined with lead. Pope Gregory the Great defended pictures as teaching those who cannot read.

cards.headline: At the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, the walls are made of Bible stories.
cards.body: This royal chapel, consecrated in 1248, has 1,113 stained-glass scenes, so many that the walls seem to be made of glass. Level 26's flying buttresses freed walls to become windows. So how do you build a window from colored light, and why fill it with stories?

cards.headline: Color cooked into the glass
cards.body: Medieval glassmakers colored glass while it was molten, by adding metal oxides: cobalt, for instance, gives a deep blue. The glazier cut the colored sheets into pieces, painted faces and folds of cloth with a dark paint made partly of ground glass, and fired them in a kiln so the paint fused on. Strips of lead called cames held the pieces together, like a jigsaw with the joins left showing.

cards.fact: One window at Chartres survived the fire of 1194.
cards.context: Fire destroyed most of Chartres Cathedral in 1194. The central panels of the Virgin and Child in the window called Notre-Dame de la Belle Verrière, made about 1180, survived and were set into the new building. For centuries, this image of Mary has been an object of special veneration.

cards.headline: Pictures for people who can't read
cards.body: Why fill windows with stories? In a letter of 600, Pope Gregory the Great defended religious pictures: what writing gives those who read, a picture gives to those who can't. His argument remained the standard defense of religious images in the Western church through the Middle Ages. A window was a page anyone could read, as long as the sun was out.

mascot.line: Keep this argument in mind: pictures teach people who can't read. Level 78 makes it again.

cards.headline: Stained glass: made
learned: Metal oxides color glass while it is molten
Painted details are fired on; lead cames join the pieces
Chartres' Belle Verrière survived the fire of 1194
Gregory the Great: pictures teach those who cannot read

questions.prompt: What held the pieces of a medieval stained-glass window together?

options.label: Wooden frames carved for each piece
options.rationale: Wood didn't join the pieces; lead did.

options.label: Paint fired in a kiln
options.rationale: The fired paint added details, not joins.

options.label: A layer of clear glass on top
options.rationale: That describes gold tesserae, not windows.

questions.explanation: Lead strips called cames held the cut pieces of glass together.

questions.prompt: How did Pope Gregory the Great defend religious pictures?

options.label: They let people who couldn't read learn the stories
They made churches warmer in winter
options.rationale: His argument was about teaching, not comfort.

options.label: They proved the church was wealthy
options.rationale: He argued pictures teach, not that they impress.

questions.explanation: Gregory wrote that a picture gives those who cannot read what writing gives those who can.

questions.prompt: Why did Level 26's flying buttresses matter so much for stained glass?

options.label: They were decorated with glass panels
options.rationale: The buttresses are stone; the windows are between them.

options.label: They reflected sunlight into the church
options.rationale: Their job was structural, not optical.

options.label: They made colored glass cheaper to melt
options.rationale: Glassmaking didn't change; the walls did.

options.label: They freed walls to become large windows

questions.explanation: Flying buttresses took the vault's outward push, so walls could be thin and filled with glass.
